title: Spec: Commit gates for any repository
text: jlog and the log: In a new repository with no language, just check passes, and the run log shows each step as skipped. In a new Python repository and a new TypeScript repository, just check runs the real steps, and a failed step stops the commit. Each line of each step, in the root Justfile and in the modules, is in the run log. A repository with set shell := ["bash", "-c"] keeps working, after the person wraps it as ["jlog", "bash", "-c"]. The lint finds a shebang step, a - line and a [no-cd] step. .agents/log/ stays after git add -A, git stash -u and git clean -fd. A worktree with only a log folder can be pruned. A backtick line is tagged "kind": "backtick". A secret from a .env file does not appear in line or argv. jlog tools logs the versions, and a missing program does not fail a line. The cost of each line over the shell itself is measured and reported. The pass: No pass is written for just --no-deps check, for JUST_NO_DEPS=true just check, for just v=x check, for jlog pass run directly, or with an unstaged change. A skip of a step that an installed profile provides fails the pass. The lab of jlog uses a stub profile for it. JUST_COLOR=always just check can pass. The commit tree: git commit -a by an agent stops if the records cover only the staged files. A commit with partial staging stops, and the gate prints the fix with git stash --keep-index -u. The first commit of a new repository works with the default list. git merge runs the gate through the pre-merge-commit hook. Records: An agent commit with no review record for the tree stops. The chain update-docs, prose, test-review, review and check passes, and so does the chain with review before test-review. A chain with prose before update-docs stops. A record with status failed, or with a finding that is not fixed, does not count. A review by a fresh agent in another worktree gives a record that the gate finds. just record-skip review "typo" asks the person, then lets one tree through, and the run log keeps the reason. The text of .agents/targets/review.md appears in the review packet. jagt render saves packets/ .json with the target, the input tree, the path of the worktree and the hash of the packet. A result with another nonce, or with none, gives no record. The record shows the model of the fresh agent, in Claude Code and in Codex. The same review gate works in Claude Code and in Codex. just visual-check and just visualize each write a packet that jagt lint accepts. Sessions and the environment: In Codex, each line in the run log has the thread ID, and jlog session gives the path of the transcript. In Claude Code, each line has the session ID, and the lines of a fresh agent are marked as such. At a terminal, all just calls in one terminal share one session. jlog env shows any secret as redacted. No plugin writes in the folders of a harness. A recipe that needs a setting from .zshrc fails the lab, with a message that names set export or .env. Setup: The installer stops with the install line when a program in the tools table is missing. just install run by an agent writes a packet with the open questions. After just install --answer issues=none, that question is not asked again. In CI, the installer takes the defaults and asks nothing. No hook, skill or doc of agent_gest_git_skills names GitButler or but. A stacked PR with plain git and gh passes the gates. Hooks: The hook that stops a commit says which target or step to run. git commit -m "fix" --no-verify by an agent stops. An empty required.txt in the commit does not remove the review. A test suite that runs git in temporary repositories does not break the commit, because the gate does not run the steps. In a Python, a TypeScript and a Rust project, the gate runs as a local hook of the pre-commit framework. Removing the lint tool keeps the gate. The turn gate of nossaifd: A page that just prose passed, in any worktree, does not block the end of a later turn. A page with a recorded pass and no prose record still stops a commit that needs a prose record. With the tasker role installed, the Stop block says “run just prose”. When the tasker role is installed, nossaifd-prose.yml is removed. Without it, the file stays as now. A reinstall of nossaifd after the tasker role does not bring back nossaifd-prose.yml. With the tasker role, the project gets .github/workflows/check.yml. Its job checks out the head of the pull request with fetch-depth: 0 and runs just ci. A commit with no trailer of the gate fails it. A CI file of the person stays as it is, and the file stays after just uninstall. Each commit that passes the gate gets a Commit-Gate trailer. ci-gate passes it, also after a rebase with no conflict. It fails a commit made with git commit -n, and a commit changed after the gate passed it. just ci runs ci-gate and the steps of the list ci. A name in the list that is not a step of just check is left out, with a message. The gate guard stops the plain forms of --no-verify, -n, core.hooksPath and a write to a protected path. It lets a command that hides git run, such as bash <<EOF or python -c. Its tests list both kinds. prose-check and the turn gate accept the same pages, a .qmd file included. A change to CHANGELOG.md alone needs no prose record. The removal of the GitButler Stop hook keeps the nossaifd Stop hook. Tests and docstrings: In each of the three profiles, a changed line that no test runs fails coverage-check. In Python and TypeScript, a pragma on that line makes it pass. In Rust, an entry for its file in the exclude list makes it pass. A line that only integration runs passes coverage-check when integration is in just check. A commit that adds its own path to generated.txt or coverage-exclude.txt still fails coverage-check. So does a commit that creates one of these files with its own path in it. In a project with no .agents/generated.txt or .agents/coverage-exclude.txt, coverage-check, docstring-check and the gate act as with empty lists. A missing file fails none of them. When code changed and there is no coverage report, coverage-check fails and says “write tests”. For a change with Rust unit tests only, test-parent does not call test-paths, and it records “no test ran on the parent”, not a pass. A runner that crashes on the parent gives “the runner failed” in the result of test-parent, not a failure of the test. A new test in an existing test file that fails on the parent commit makes test-parent exit with 0, and its result file names the test. A commit that removes a language from .agents/stack.json still needs a test-review record for the code of that language. No hook, skill or doc of agent_gest_git_skills names ruff, biome, pytest or another tool of a language. In a repository with no just check, each skill of the table in “The skills” tells the agent to run gsu. In just check, the tests of each language run once, and the run log shows one JLOG_RUN for all lines. jlog pass finds each step of just check when the index runs the steps in inner just calls. A recipe of a module shows the JLOG_RUN of the root. JLOG_RUN set by hand to the ID of an old run of another tree gives no pass, and coverage-check does not read that run’s report. coverage-check does not read a report with another run ID. So just coverage-check alone runs the tests again. In Rust, an item with no doc in a file of generated.txt passes docstring-check, and one outside it fails, with its file and line. A path in .agents/generated.txt fails neither coverage-check nor docstring-check. On the first commit, coverage-check runs the report tool of the profile over all code with a limit of 100%, and test-parent is a skip. just check in a fresh clone leaves no file that git does not ignore. In each of the three profiles, a private function with no doc fails docstring-check, and the output names its file and line. A commit that changes code and has no test-review record stops. A commit that changes only docs needs no test-review record. test-review gives a finding for a new test that passes on the parent commit, and for a new pragma with no reason. The review packet has the docs lens, and a stub doc such as “Returns the result.” gives a finding. The update-docs packet of a Python project holds the Python language layer. A new Rust project gets just check with real steps, and no api step. Docs: A new Python project with the docs tool has the api tool, and a public function with no docments fails just check. Until the smalldocs release that reads JSDoc, a new TypeScript project with the docs tool passes just check, with no api step. prose-check runs prose_gate.py check-changed on the changed pages, the files that is_page accepts, and writes nothing into the repository. A page that .agents/nossaifd-checkers.json maps to another checker gets that checker. When prose_gate.py or its checker is missing, the step fails and prints the install line. With the nossaifd role, the role file fills prose-check. just --summary parses, and just prose-check runs the recipe of the role file, not a no-op step. Without the role, prose-check is a no-op step. A change with no page passes prose-check, and so does the first commit of a repository with no page. A commit that adds a page with a hard problem does not pass the gate. With prose-check in the list ci, CI also runs the step on the pull request. With CI=1 on a machine, a page with a hard problem that is not committed yet still fails prose-check. A repository with its own test recipe, and no set allow-duplicate-recipes, still gets the combined recipes and the no-op steps of the other names. Two runs of just install in a row write the same index. In a Python project with the api tool, prose-check also checks the API pages of each changed module, through a temporary file. In CI, just docs-publish pushes to gh-pages for a public repository. It skips a private repository, and it fails in CI when gh has no token.

title: The tools
text: Each tool of the profile brings its recipes. No tool adds a crate to Cargo.toml. The tools use cargo, uv, and the programs that the key programs of profile.json names. The installer installs each of those with rustup or cargo. The recipes have no shebang line, so each line of a recipe runs through the shell of its module, .agents/just/rust.just. When that module sets jlog as its shell, the run log has each line. A set shell in the root Justfile does not reach the recipes of a module. The steps run cargo with --locked, so a step never makes or changes Cargo.lock. Run just setup to make the file or to bring it up to date, and commit it. The steps also run with --all-features, so the code behind each feature counts. Code behind a feature that cannot be on together with another feature, or code for another platform, such as #[cfg(windows)] on macOS, does not count.

title: The tools
text: Every project of the profile gets the base, even a project with no tool. Recipe What it does just setup Downloads every dependency with cargo fetch, and makes or updates Cargo.lock just build Builds every package of the workspace. Extra arguments go to cargo: just build --release just version Prints the version of the project, X.Y.Z, from [package] or [workspace.package] of the root Cargo.toml, for the release tag. It prints nothing when there is none. It exits with 2 when the file cannot be read, or when the version is not semver. It is not a step of just check The base adds /target/ and *.profraw to .gitignore, and /target/ to .worktreedisposable. The leading / keeps a module folder such as src/target/ in git. That file lists the ignored files that a command can make again. Every report of a step goes to target/, so a step leaves no file that git sees.

title: The tools
text: toml is not a default tool. Install it with just install toml. It needs taplo and cargo-sort, and the installer installs both with cargo +stable install --locked. Recipe What it does just toml-fmt Sorts the tables of each Cargo.toml of the workspace with cargo sort --workspace --no-format, then formats the TOML files with taplo fmt just toml-check Checks both, and changes no file toml-check is not a step of the commit gates. So just verify runs it, and just check and the commit gate do not. A CI job that wants it runs just rust toml-check. cargo-sort reads its config tomlfmt.toml from the top of the project. When that file is missing and .config/tomlfmt.toml exists, the recipe passes that file with --config. taplo gets only the TOML files that git tracks or does not ignore, so it never reads target/. cargo-sort only sorts, because its format of arrays differs from that of taplo.

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just fmt Formats the code of every package with cargo fmt --all just fmt-check Checks the format with cargo fmt --all --check, and changes no file just lint Runs cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings. Extra arguments go to cargo: just lint -p app

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just typecheck Checks the types of the code and the tests with cargo check --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just test Runs the unit tests, those of the libraries and the binaries, with cargo llvm-cov test. It writes the coverage to target/llvm-cov/test.lcov. Extra arguments go to cargo llvm-cov test, so just test parse runs the unit tests whose names hold parse just coverage-check Fails on each changed line of code that no test runs. A line that test or integration runs passes. It runs each of them first, unless it wrote its report in the same run just test-paths [PATH...] Runs the tests of some files in the folder tests, with cargo test and without coverage cargo llvm-cov writes the coverage as an LCOV file, a text format that lists how often each line ran. diff-cover is a Python program that compares such a file with the diff of git. coverage-check runs diff-cover against HEAD, with a limit of 100%. The diff holds the staged, the unstaged and the untracked changes. An untracked path that is not a file, such as a link to a folder, does not count. The jnterfaces installer makes such a link, .claude/skills/rust-profile. diff-cover cannot read it, so the step leaves it out. Such a path whose name holds a \ stops the step. diff-cover reads each \ as a /, so to leave out that path it would leave out other files too. Rename it, remove it or add it to .gitignore. The step merges the report of test and that of integration into one report, and gives it to diff-cover. A line that one of them runs passes. A line that one report measures and no report runs fails, also when the other report does not measure it, as for code under #[cfg(not(test))]. It reads each report only for the same run ID and the same worktree tree. The build of the coverage run stays warm between checks. Cargo compiles again only what the change needs: Before each run, the step removes the .profraw files of the last run. So a count from an old run, such as that of a deleted test, never counts. The step cleans each workspace package that holds a changed Rust file, so the compiler runs on that file and gives its module evidence. It also cleans each workspace package that depends on such a package. A test binary holds the code of each package that it depends on. The step test does not build the integration tests again. Their old binaries would keep the old code, and llvm-cov could take their counts for the new lines. The dependencies come from the resolved graph of cargo metadata, so a path crate outside the workspace and a [patch] count too. The others stay as they are. A crate outside those packages may compile a changed file, through #[path] or include!. Its dep-info file, which rustc writes beside the build, then lists the file, and the step cleans the whole workspace. A changed file that is not Rust code, but that a dep-info file lists, cleans the whole workspace too. So does a failed cargo metadata. The step cleans the whole workspace on the first run, with no parent commit, and when the fingerprint of the build changes. The fingerprint holds these: the versions of rustc and cargo llvm-cov; each variable whose name starts with CARGO or RUST; each Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain and the cargo config. A change of one can give each test binary a new name, and the old binary would stay beside the new one. Its lines would then count as lines that no test runs. A build may have a folder of its own, from build.build-dir, CARGO_LLVM_COV_TARGET_DIR or CARGO_LLVM_COV_BUILD_DIR. Then the step cleans the whole workspace on each run. The dependency builds stay in each case. The step saves the fingerprint in target/llvm-cov-target after a run passes. A failed run leaves no fingerprint, and the next run cleans the whole workspace. So does a run with extra arguments, such as --config. On the first commit of a repository, diff-cover has no parent to compare with. Then the step checks each line of the merged report, and it names each line that no test runs. The report of integration counts only when integration is in the steps of just check. The installer of jnterfaces writes those steps into the key steps of .agents/stack.json. The setup answer that runs integration only in just verify takes it out of that list. Then a line that only an integration test runs fails coverage-check. Give it a unit test, or exclude its file. With no .agents/stack.json, the report counts, as the spec says by default. diff-cover counts only the files that are in the report. cargo llvm-cov leaves out a file that no test target compiles, such as a file that no mod line names, or a file in examples/. It also leaves out each file in a folder named tests, examples or benches, at any depth, for example src/tests/mod.rs. So coverage-check also fails on each changed .rs file that is not in the report. The exceptions are the files in the folder tests or benches of a package, the files of the two lists, and files that pass the declaration check below. On the first commit, the step checks only the files in the reports. The build script build.rs is in the report. The declaration check parses the whole current file with tree-sitter 0.25.2 and its Rust grammar 0.24.0. It accepts imports, modules and type declarations, including empty files. It rejects handwritten functions, impls, initializers, macros, syntax errors and unknown syntax or attributes. It accepts only the exact #[cfg(test)] marker on modules and imports, and #[allow(unused_imports)] on imports. Parser or file errors retain the missing-file failure. The step also needs module evidence from a successful compiler call in the current test run. It records fresh compiler dependencies with source hashes. A module path from that compiler target must reach the file. The path may use plain module declarations or exact #[cfg(test)] module declarations when the compiler call has --test. Other conditional or attributed module paths and files read only as data do not qualify. A pre-existing compiler wrapper still runs, but cannot supply module evidence because it may return cached output. The run, worktree and source hashes must still match. Each accepted absent file prints its category and module evidence; it has no authored executable source to measure. An LCOV record with a zero count still fails under the usual rules. Known Clap derives (Args, Subcommand, ValueEnum, Parser) and built-in derives may qualify. The check resolves explicit Clap imports and rejects shadowed or unknown derives. Known helper attributes accept literals, named paths, literal lists and ranges; calls, closures, blocks and macros fail. A named parser callback keeps its own coverage obligation in its source file. Generated parser behavior still needs tests and macro review. The known derives also include serde::Deserialize, serde::Serialize and getset::Getters, with unambiguous explicit imports or aliases. #[serde(default)] qualifies only on a struct with the known Deserialize derive; #[get = "pub"] qualifies only on a field of a struct with the known Getters derive. Other Serde and getset helpers, including configured callbacks, retain the failure. On an enum, the exact inert lint attribute #[allow(clippy::enum_variant_names)] qualifies. Unknown, shadowed or ambiguous names retain the failure, and generated serialization and getter behavior still needs tests. LLVM counts the code of a macro_rules! macro at the line that calls the macro. So a branch of a macro that no test runs does not fail coverage-check, and the test-review target checks it.

title: The tools
text: The root Justfile of a project has the line export JLOG_RUN := env("JLOG_RUN", uuid()). So each run of just, such as just check, has one run ID, and each inner call of just gets the same ID. A module must not have the line, because a second line would make a second ID. A full run of just test, with no arguments, takes the worktree tree before the tests run. The worktree tree is the tree hash of every file that git does not ignore, staged or not, without the folder target. When the tests pass and the tree has not changed, test saves JLOG_RUN and the tree in target/llvm-cov/test.run.json. A file that changed while the tests ran drops the run, because the report may come from the old code. coverage-check reads a report only when both match the current run and the current tree. So in just check, which runs test, then integration, then coverage-check, the tests run once. Alone, just coverage-check runs the tests itself, and so does a run after just test parse. integration saves its run in the same way, in target/llvm-cov/integration.run.json.

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just integration Runs the integration tests with cargo llvm-cov test: each test target, and each example or bench that sets test = true. It writes the coverage to target/llvm-cov/integration.lcov. Extra arguments go to cargo llvm-cov test, as for test An integration test is a test target, such as a file tests/NAME.rs, or a [[test]] of Cargo.toml. It uses the crate from outside, as a user does. A workspace with no test target runs no test, and its report is empty. Each step reads the targets from cargo metadata, and names each target whose key test is true, with --bin, --test, --example or --bench. So a [[test]] with test = false, such as a slow suite, does not run, as with a plain cargo test. A library has no such name, so test gives --lib. cargo looks for a name in each package. So when a library sets test = false, or two packages have a target of the same name and only one tests it, each package runs in a cargo llvm-cov of its own, and the step merges the reports. An extra argument that chooses targets or packages, such as --test api or -p core, takes the place of the choice of the step. The step adds --workspace only when the arguments choose no package. So just integration --test slow runs that suite, and just test --test api runs only tests/api.rs. An argument after -- goes to the tests. The doctests, the tests in doc comments, run in neither step. cargo llvm-cov test leaves them out unless it gets --doctests, and that option needs nightly Rust.

title: The tools
text: test-paths takes the files that the test-parent recipe of the tasker role gives it. test-parent gives it only the changed files that match the key tests of profile.json, tests/**. When no file matches, as in a change with unit tests only, test-parent does not call test-paths. A unit test lives in the file of its code, such as src/lib.rs, and a copy of that file in the parent commit would bring the new code too. A file tests/NAME.rs runs as its test target. Any other file in the folder tests, such as tests/common/mod.rs, runs every test target of that folder. When called by hand with a file of code, test-paths skips the file and says so. The exit code of test-paths tells test-parent what happened. Each profile gives the same four codes: 0 means the tests ran and passed. 1 means a test failed or did not build. A new test of new code often does not build on the parent, and that is a failure of the test. 5 means no test ran. The files may hold only code and no test file, the test targets may hold no test, or the folder tests may have no test target. A test with #[ignore] does not run, so it does not count. With no path, test-paths runs no test and exits with 5. pytest gives the same code when it collects no test. 2 means the run itself failed. cargo may fail, for example on a stale Cargo.lock or on a path that it cannot run. Or a test may end the run, as with std::process::exit in a test, before its binary gives a result. test-paths runs the tests of each package, and then gives one code. A failed test in any package gives 1, even when another package’s run ended early. A dependency whose build script fails for an outside reason, such as a missing system library, gives 1, not 2. cargo prints the same lines as for a test that does not build. The spec lists this as a limit of the Rust profile. cargo exits with 101 both when a test fails or does not build and when it fails itself. So test-paths reads the error lines of cargo to tell them apart. test-paths reads the output of cargo to count the tests that ran. So it runs cargo with no colors and with neither quiet nor verbose output, whatever the settings of CARGO_TERM_COLOR, CARGO_TERM_QUIET and CARGO_TERM_VERBOSE. A target with harness = false prints no count, so its run counts as a test that ran. test-paths reads the name of each test target from cargo metadata. So a [[test]] with a name other than its file still runs. A file in tests that is no test target, as with autotests = false, does not run, and test-paths says so. A test binary that names its tests and then stops with no result ends the run early. That happens on std::process::exit(0) or std::process::exit(1) in a test. test-paths then gives 2, as the spec says for every language, and not 1. A test that libtest names as failed before the stop still gives 1. A stop also ends the rest of the run of its package, so a test that would fail in a later binary of that package does not run. The key tests of profile.json names tests/**, the folder tests at the top of the project. A glob cannot name only the folder tests of each package of a workspace, because **/tests/** also takes a module such as src/x/tests/mod.rs, whose new code would reach the parent. So the tests of a member package are not copied to the parent, and test-review judges them from the diff.

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just docstring-check Fails on each item with no doc comment, public or private, and names its file and line The step runs cargo clippy with the lints missing_docs and clippy::missing_docs_in_private_items, with every feature. It checks the code of the libraries and the binaries, and not the tests. As the spec says, the step gives the two lints with -W, not -D, and reads the JSON messages of clippy. It has two reasons. An error in a library stops clippy from checking the binaries that use it, and a generated file must not fail the step. The step also passes --cap-lints warn. So a crate that sets #![deny(missing_docs)] still gets the list of items, and a generated file in such a crate still passes. An item in a file that git ignores, such as code that build.rs writes into target/, counts as generated. An #[allow(missing_docs)] in the code wins over the lints of the command line, so it hides its items from the step. The review target checks each new #[allow]. Each line of its output has the form src/lib.rs:18:4: missing documentation for a function.

title: The tools
text: Recipe What it does just api-check Fails on each public item, parameter and return with no comment for the API pages, then runs api-prose-check just api-prose-check [--base REF] Checks the API page of each changed file with the checker of nossaifd The recipes have the names and the form of the api tools of the Python and TypeScript profiles. The step docs-check of the docs role runs api-check, and so does just verify. api-check runs smalldocs api check of smalldocs 0.5.12 with uv. smalldocs reads the API with cargo +nightly-2026-11-12 rustdoc, which writes the JSON format 61. smalldocs reads only the formats 57 and 61, so the profile pins the date. The program nightly of the tool installs that toolchain with rustup toolchain install nightly-2026-11-12 --profile minimal. Its check is rustup run nightly-2026-11-12 rustc --version, which never downloads a toolchain. rustup toolchain list and rustup show active-toolchain would install a missing pin of the project. The step fails on three things: A public item with no doc comment. A parameter with no comment after it on its line, and no line in an # Arguments section. A return other than () with no # Returns section. When docs/_smalldocs.yml has the key api with a section that says language: rust, the step checks only those sections. A section with no toolchain gets the pin. Otherwise the step checks each package of the workspace that has a library or a binary. A crate with only a binary gets the pages of its private items, as smalldocs does. api-prose-check builds the API pages into a temporary folder, outside the project. It then runs the checker of nossaifd on the page of each changed API file and on the module comment of that file, the //! lines at its top. A changed file changed since HEAD. In CI, or with --base REF, it changed since the base that check-changed of nossaifd takes. Without the prose role, which installs the checker, the step passes. A run that passed is not run again in the same run of just, on the same tree and with the same base. The run files of api-prose-check go into .jnprofile-rust/, as those of the Python and TypeScript profiles go into .jnprofile-python/ and .jnprofile-typescript/. The tool adds the folder to .gitignore and .worktreedisposable. .agents/just/rust/api_rule.py holds the rule of the commit gate for the API files. Its function is_api(path) is true for a file that rustdoc reads for the pages. It is false in a project without the tool api or without the docs role, as .agents/stack.json records them. When the rule cannot read the api settings, such as a key api written on one line, it is true for each Rust file outside the folders of the tools and .agents/generated.txt. So the gate stays on, as with the rules of the Python and TypeScript profiles. With the key api in docs/_smalldocs.yml, the crates are those of its Rust sections. A manifest names a crate from docs/, and a section with no manifest takes the Cargo.toml of its root, as smalldocs does. Without the key, the crate of a file is the nearest folder above it with a Cargo.toml. In a crate with a library, the files are src/lib.rs and the modules under src/. In a crate with only a binary, they are src/main.rs and its modules. The binaries in src/bin/, the tests, the examples, build.rs and the files of .agents/generated.txt are not API files. The rule reads no TOML, so a library at another path, with path in [lib], does not count. api-prose-check takes its changed files by the same rule, without the check of the tool and the role.

title: The tools
section: Lines that no test can run
text: Stable Rust has no pragma that leaves out one line from the coverage. So the profile reads two lists of files: .agents/coverage-exclude.txt lists the files that coverage-check leaves out. .agents/generated.txt lists the generated files. Both coverage-check and docstring-check leave them out. Each line of a list is a path or a glob, with the rules of git pathspecs. A * does not match a /, ** matches any number of folders, and a path that ends with / names a folder. A line that starts with # is a comment. Write the reason for each entry in a comment above it. The steps read both lists from the parent commit, with git show HEAD:./PATH, which names the path from the top of the project. So a new entry counts only after it is in a commit of its own, and a commit cannot exempt its own code. With no parent, or when the parent has no such file, the list is empty. The test-review target judges each new entry.

title: The tools
text: The recipes of coverage-check, docstring-check, test-paths and api-check run .agents/just/rust/steps.py with uv. The script needs Python 3.11 or later. The installed recipes resolve the pinned tree-sitter runtime and Rust grammar with uv run --with; the parser helper ships beside steps.py. The package test command uses the same pins. The api commands run it again under smalldocs, whose PyYAML reads docs/_smalldocs.yml. It reads the lists from the parent commit, and it leaves the excluded files out of a copy of the coverage report, in target/jnprofile-rust/. It also reads the JSON messages of clippy, and prints each item with no doc. coverage-check runs diff-cover 11.0.1 with uv run --with.
